newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian budget expected to win parliament battle.
newsitem.headline: Italian budget expected to win parliament battle.

text.p: Italy's 1997 budget enters the turbulent Chamber of Deputies on Thursday with the government bracing itself to use confidence motions to blast away heavy opposition to the austerity package.
Analysts say Prime Minister Romano Prodi should chalk up an easy victory, adding that swift ratification would help propel the lira back into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).

The budget aims to slash a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's projected deficit and was drawn up in a hurried effort to win debt-laden Italy membership of Europe's planned single currency from the launch in 1999.

Unveiled last month, the budget has battled its way through numerous commissions in the lower house of parliament largely unscathed but thousands of amendments await it in the full chamber along with expected filibustering.

"We're going to obstruct this bill and the only way the government is going to get it past us is by using confidence votes," the bellicose leader of the separatist Northern League party, Umberto Bossi, said at the weekend.
Prodi, who has been in office six months and has already resorted to the life-or-death confidence motion twice to by-pass League obstructionism, has indicated he is ready to do so again.

Despite falling short of a clear majority in the lower house, Prodi's centre-left coalition can expect the support of the hardleft Communist Refoundation and ensure that the budget is approved on schedule by November 14.
After this it will pass for a further reading to the Senate (upper house), but this is expected to be a formality.
"All in all it will be a smoother passage than budgets in previous years have had," said Lorenzo Stanca, head of research at bank Credito Italiano in Milan.

Prodi has pledged that as soon as the bill has cleared the lower chamber he will initiate intensive negotiations to put the lira back into the ERM before the end of December -- four years after it was thrown out of the grid during a currency crisis.
Many in the market believe this is an achievable goal and a step along the road to becoming a founder member of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Prodi insists his budget, one of the toughest seen in post-war Italy which includes a special one-off "Euro Tax" designed to raise at least 11.5 trillion lire, will be enough to propel the country along the rest of that arduous road.

A number of senior German bankers expressed doubts earlier this month about whether the package would pare back Italy's meaty state deficit to the required level. Opposition parties concur, adding that it will plunge the economy into recession.
Investors however are betting that the financial bill will push Italy to the gates of EMU if not directly inside, and market rates have fallen considerably over the past month.

"It seems that the budget will have a very positive impact on helping Italy reach the Maastricht criteria," said Gregorio De Felice, chief economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana said of the tough European Union criteria for EMU.
"On the other hand it will have a negative impact of around 0.5 percent on economic growth," he added.

The government confidently predicts that the package will have a minimal impact on the flagging economy, but is already concerned about what will happen in 1998, when the battery of one-off measures in the budget have been fired.

Calls are steadily growing for an overhaul of the welfare state along with another review of the costly pensions system. Aware that any major strucutural changes will take months of negotiations to achieve, ministers are preparing to bring forward preparation of the 1998 budget.

"Instead of considering the 1998 budget at the end of 1997, we will discuss it in the first half of next year and it will include a possible revision of the pensions system," Lanfranco Turci, the head of economic research in the largest government party, the PDS, told Reuters Financial Television last week.
